repos.title: RoboScope Kit: Unified Interfaces for Fast and Scalable Embodied-AI Evaluation
repos.paper_summary: RoboScope Kit is a shared evaluation layer for robot-policy benchmarks. Each model is wrapped once as a Policy class, and each benchmark is wrapped once as an adapter around its native evaluator, so benchmark rules and scoring stay unchanged. A scheduler runs simulator workers and Policy replicas as separate pools, sizes both with a time-bounded concurrency search over short probes, and shards work deterministically across GPU instances. Runtime optimization renders only the observations a chunked Policy reads. Adapters cover six benchmark families. On LIBERO-Long with a StarVLA checkpoint on one RTX 4090, the search selects twelve workers and three replicas, which evaluate 500 episodes 4.45× faster than the official StarVLA evaluator, with equivalent success rates. With CUDA MPS, sixteen workers and four replicas give 6.16× speedup. On RoboTwin Easy, four GPUs with chunk-boundary observation finish 500 episodes in 14.4 minutes, 25.04× faster than the single-GPU baseline, with identical success outcomes and terminal steps. The speedups are measured against the official evaluators and the baselines named in the paper, and the evidence covers two benchmarks in detail. Search time adds 506 s on LIBERO-Long.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: RoboScope Kit wraps models and benchmarks once and separates simulator workers from model replicas to speed evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and Motivation
digest_headlines.headline: The official StarVLA evaluator leaves the GPU at 14.3% average utilization because simulation and per-step handling dominate CPU time.

digest_headlines.heading: Design
digest_headlines.headline: The design separates simulator workers from Policy replicas and uses a diagonal search to size both from measured probes.

digest_headlines.heading: Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The implementation packages a Python Policy API, native benchmark evaluators, and a six-family adapter catalog that run as separate local processes.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: RoboScope Kit matches official LIBERO-Long outcomes and evaluates 4.45 times faster than StarVLA, and 6.16 times faster with CUDA MPS.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: The related work places the paper among evaluation harnesses and simulation engines that separate simulators from inference.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Search cost is large on short workloads, so reporting search time beside evaluation time shows when automation pays off.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The system matches official outcomes and cuts evaluation time 4.45 to 6.16 times on LIBERO-Long, and 359.7 to 14.4 minutes on RoboTwin Easy.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists Policy lifecycle methods, benchmark contracts, work-queue states, experimental details, tuning runs, and adapter catalog.

repos.title: LongBanana: An Expert-Verified Benchmark for Long-Context Multi-Reference Image Synthesis
repos.paper_summary: LongBanana is a benchmark of 90 expert-designed, expert-verified tasks for synthesizing one image from many reference images, with 4,670 atomic checklist items. Tasks average about 32 references and include hard-negative references that must be excluded. Each task is converted into an entity–relation graph, and items are scored on Content Fidelity, Relational Binding, and Global Constraint Satisfaction by LongBananaEval, an agentic judge that calls tools such as OCR and counting. Reviewers labeled 46,700 item judgments; a 15% double-labeled subset reached 89.4% exact agreement and 0.83 quadratic weighted kappa. On output-level Overall scores, LongBananaEval reaches Pearson 0.8707, versus 0.8413 for a single-pass VLM judge. For generation, the paper compares direct prompting, agent harnesses, and RPR workflows, with Nano Banana 2 as the image generator. The best system, OpenClaw + RPR, scores 78.4 average and 47.8 P@70%, against 74.6 and 35.6 for PD-Direct, a baseline given the construction graph. RPR gains depend on the harness, and the paper notes it can introduce drift.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Multi-reference image generation errors are provenance failures that holistic realism scores cannot localize.

digest_headlines.heading: The LongBanana Benchmark
digest_headlines.headline: LongBanana contains 90 cases across a 3-by-3 taxonomy, each scored through atomic graph-derived checklist items.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Nano Banana 2 under OpenClaw with RPR scores 78.4 overall, above the 68.4 of full-prompt direct generation.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Agentic workflows reach broader success than a fixed privileged schedule, and checklist scores localize failures.

digest_headlines.heading: Acknowledgments and Disclosure of Funding
digest_headlines.headline: Funding comes from two Guangdong programs and KlingAI Research, and the authors declare no other competing interests.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers related work, benchmark construction details, scorer and label quality statistics, extra experiments, and release safeguards.

repos.title: TailSteer: Trajectory-Tail Steering for Drift-Resistant Multi-turn Image Editing
repos.paper_summary: TailSteer is a final-stage training framework that reduces cumulative drift in multi-turn image editing by steering only the late denoising steps of a base editor. The refined model is trained on its own on-policy rollouts, using unchanged source content as a preservation reference, so no curated ground-truth editing pairs are needed. Early steps are trained to match the frozen base model's velocity. Later steps blend that velocity with a preservation velocity toward a source-based endpoint, with the blend weight falling from 1 at the steering onset to 0 at the final step. The method is tested on FLUX.1 Kontext [dev], FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT, and Qwen-Image-2.1. The paper reports substantially reduced drift over 15 to 20 editing turns. On FLUX.2 [klein] Base 9B, Qwen-IB EN changes by at most +0.47 across the tested steering onsets. Limitations: drift is measured only over 15 to 20 turns, training uses only identity and local edit families, and qualitative comparisons use one steering onset.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: One-shot editors accumulate small errors across repeated turns, so strong single-turn editing does not guarantee long-horizon editing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior fixes add modules, change representations, or add memory, whereas TailSteer trains the base model's own denoising dynamics.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: TailSteer trains a copy of the base model on its own rollouts, steering only late denoising steps toward source-preserving endpoints.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: Across four backbones, TailSteer reduces drift over 15–20 editing turns while keeping single-turn scores close to base models.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The conclusion says TailSteer reduces cumulative drift across FLUX, SenseNova, and Qwen while largely retaining base generative capabilities.

repos.title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
repos.paper_summary: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness, Tilapia, for having AI agents build machine-checked TLA+ proofs of properties of real-world system specifications using the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS). The benchmark has 265 proof targets from 95 specifications; the evaluation uses an active set of 70 targets across 12 specifications. Tilapia gives agents TLAPS, the SANY parser, the TLC and Apalache model checkers, and proof libraries. It accepts a proof only if the target statement and specification are unchanged, every lemma the target transitively depends on is proved, and the proof passes grading in a fresh container with the original tools. The highest-scoring configuration, GPT-6.1 Sol (Codex) at max effort, proved 31 of 70 targets (44.3%, pass@3), at a total cost of USD 328.86. Other configurations scored 34.3% to 42.9%. The agents proved properties for specifications such as Bosco, the German protocol, and several write-ahead logs. The authors report 46 specification issues found during task construction, 35 of which were fixed. Limitations: the evaluation covers only 70 targets and two frontier model families; the paper reports that naive calls to automated backends are ineffective, and that invariant choice strongly affects proof difficulty.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: TLAPS-Bench tests whether AI agents can build end-to-end machine-checked TLA+ proofs for real-world system specifications.

digest_headlines.heading: Background
digest_headlines.headline: TLA+ theorems are accepted only when TLAPS verifies the proof, while model checkers help test candidate invariants.

digest_headlines.heading: Tilapia: TLA+ Proof Harness
digest_headlines.headline: Tilapia gives agents proof tools and blocks cheating by making targets read-only and grading in a clean container.

digest_headlines.heading: TLAPS-Bench
digest_headlines.headline: The benchmark holds 95 specifications and 265 targets, and evaluation uses an active set of 70 targets from 12 specifications.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: GPT-6.1 Sol at max effort proved 31 of 70 targets (44.3%), and all models failed on Wildfire refinement.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior benchmarks mostly supply proof structure, and the closest TLA+ benchmark supplies inductive invariants to agents.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion and Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: Abstraction and refinement across layers are expected to scale proofs, as AI lowers the cost of formal proofs.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists the retired problem set, per-target results, specification fixes with counterexamples, and the agent prompt and skills.

repos.title: TaoMate-FVSR:Audio-Guided Facial Video Restoration
repos.paper_summary:
TaoMate-FVSR is an audio-guided facial video restoration framework for AI-generated video that also supports dubbing under replacement audio. It is a reference-guided flow model built on a Wan video DiT. Reconstruction starts from a mix of the source latent and Gaussian noise (strength 0.80 to 0.95), so the source mouth is not a fixed target. Reference frames and a four-frame motion history enter separate temporal slots. Training has two stages: visual restoration on degraded images and videos, then lip correction on degraded dubbed sources conditioned on target audio, with a SyncNet loss.

On a 150-video talking-head benchmark at 4× downsampling, it reports LPIPS 0.0793 and DISTS 0.0858, versus 0.1380 and 0.1421 for InstantRestore, and Sync-C/Sync-D of 7.413/7.561, versus 6.545/8.170 for SparkVSR. SparkVSR has higher PSNR (30.62 vs 28.67 dB) and SSIM (0.8863 vs 0.8836). On 30 replacement-audio clips, the enhanced-reference variant reaches Sync-C 8.175, versus 7.917 for the best cascade.

Limitations: the main comparison uses the ground-truth first frame as reference, and the enhanced-reference variant lowers PSNR to 23.52 dB. Native AIGC results are qualitative only.

digest_headlines.heading: 1 Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Restoring small AIGC faces requires lip and teeth detail that agrees with the spoken audio, not only sharper pixels.

digest_headlines.heading: 2 Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Related work spans facial and video restoration, generative restoration, visual dubbing, and audio-assisted restoration; the authors focus on unreliable mouths.

digest_headlines.heading: 3 Method
digest_headlines.headline: The method mixes source latents with noise to start flow reconstruction and injects sparse references and history into separate temporal slots.

digest_headlines.heading: 4 Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On the 150-video benchmark, Ours has the lowest paired perceptual error, while SparkVSR leads pixel-level fidelity.

digest_headlines.heading: 5 Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The authors state that reconstructed facial detail is a generative estimate, not evidence of true appearance, and raise impersonation risk.

repos.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
repos.paper_summary: ToolSpace is a tool-centric framework for synthesizing verifiable, long-horizon agent training tasks from real tool-call traces rather than from synthesized databases. It mines data, state, and retry dependencies between adjacent calls with deterministic rules, clusters the resulting weighted graph into 804 environments, and creates databases only for state-mutating environments. State-aware random walks with rollback build chains, which are decompiled into natural-language tasks with assertion-based checks and kept only if they replay from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and τ3-Bench Banking, the Pro versions are harder: seven frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6. The paper reports that execution-witnessed edges outperform LLM-judged ones in ablations and that performance improves with data and environment scale. The graph has 77,760 nodes, and edges are 69% data, 25% state, and 6% retry. Limitations: the paper's real-trace sources are weighted toward synthetic-tool data for some groups, and the Pro benchmarks are constructed by the same pipeline, so their difficulty reflects the method's own construction.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Data-centric synthesis derives tools after databases, so tool interfaces may not match real services; ToolSpace starts from execution traces instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior environment scaling fixes tool composition before drawing tasks, whereas ToolSpace composes tools from observed executions.

digest_headlines.heading: Preliminaries and Problem Formulation
digest_headlines.headline: Tool-centric synthesis requires walks on a typed graph whose chains replay from the initial state.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Deterministic rules build the tool graph, and only walks that replay from the initial state become training data.

digest_headlines.heading: AutomationBench Pro and $\tau^{3}$-Bench Banking Pro
digest_headlines.headline: Expert-reviewed Pro versions of two benchmarks, with 300 and 98 tasks, require more tool calls than standard splits.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: ToolSpace lifts Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6 across seven benchmarks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Conclusion restates that replay-verified, execution-witnessed composition drives gains and scales with data and environments.

repos.title: SeMo3D: Unifying 3D Generation, Editing, and Completion via Selective Modeling
repos.paper_summary: SeMo3D is a 3D diffusion model that handles generation, editing, and completion with one network by synthesizing only a selected region of a structured latent representation and leaving the rest unchanged. Training uses region-selective denoising, which applies noise and loss to randomly chosen regions of standard 3D assets, so no paired editing or completion data is needed. The architecture, Omni3DiT, is a diffusion transformer that accepts image, text, and sparse point conditions. The model is finetuned from Trellis2 at 512 resolution on Trellis-500K. On Toys4K generation, SeMo3D reports LPIPS 0.079, FID 4.99, DINO 0.926, and CD 0.0118, compared with 0.111, 5.05, 0.908, and 0.0330 for Trellis2, the image-only baseline. The provided text does not include the editing and completion tables, so this summary reports no numbers for those tasks. The paper states two limitations: the structured latent resolution cannot capture very thin structures, and the CLIP text encoder struggles with complex compositional prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Existing 3D generation, editing and completion methods regenerate whole assets, causing task isolation, altered unchanged regions and reliance on paired data.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Editing and completion methods depend on large paired datasets, and no surveyed generator jointly uses image, text and point guidance.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: The method denoises only selected latent tokens, trains on random regions of standard 3D assets, and conditions on image, text and points.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On three benchmarks, SeMo3D ranks first on most metrics for generation, editing and completion against per-task baselines.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Stated limits are coarse structured latent resolution, which misses thin palm fronds, and a text encoder that struggles with compositional prompts.

digest_headlines.heading: LLM Usage Statement
digest_headlines.headline: The statement lists uses of artificial intelligence tools for writing, code, feedback and experiments, with the authors fully responsible.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers training details, benchmark and metric definitions, inference settings, agent procedures, mask and point sensitivity tests, and extra results.

repos.title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks?
repos.paper_summary: Switch-SWE is a benchmark for whether coding agents can resume an unfinished repository task after doing other unfinished work in the same repository. It contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, each paired with an uninterrupted session and a switched session that interleaves four other unfinished tasks. Tasks are rebuilt from SWE-bench-style repair instances and from issue, pull-request, and review histories. Only the final focus patch is scored, using held-out fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass tests. Across seven model-agent configurations, switching lowers focus-task resolution by an average of 11.5 percentage points, with gaps from 6.0 to 15.0 points. Gaps are larger when interruptions touch different source directories (14.9 points) than the same ones (8.1 points). The paper also proposes a Resumption Context Manager, a plug-in for OpenCode that routes task-relevant history and keeps per-task state memory; it raises switched completion by 5.5 to 15.5 points across the evaluated models. Limitations: the locality comparison is associational because the near and far groups contain different focus tasks, and the paper does not establish the mechanism behind the locality effect.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Coding agents must resume unfinished tasks after intervening work, and existing benchmarks do not directly measure this.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work covers repository benchmarks, long-horizon development, task recovery, and context management, but not same-repository task switching.

digest_headlines.heading: Switch-SWE
digest_headlines.headline: Switch-SWE pairs each focus task with an uninterrupted control and a switched session that interleaves four other unfinished same-repository tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Results
digest_headlines.headline: Across seven configurations, switching lowers focus-task resolution by an average of 11.5 points, and far interruptions cause larger gaps than near ones.

digest_headlines.heading: Context Management for Task Resumption
digest_headlines.headline: A plug-in context manager routes task-relevant history and keeps task-state memory, and it narrows the switched-task gap on OpenCode.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Switched sessions lower resolution on average, and the proposed context manager raises switched completion on OpenCode.

digest_headlines.heading: AI use statement
digest_headlines.headline: The authors disclose their use of generative AI as coding agents, as auxiliary model components, and for writing, debugging, and figure work.

digest_headlines.heading: Ethics statement
digest_headlines.headline: The work uses repair tasks and development histories from public projects and aims to characterize agent reliability, not individual developers.

digest_headlines.heading: Reproducibility statement
digest_headlines.headline: The paper points to the sections and appendices that define construction, schedules, scoring, and the context manager, and promises a public release.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix compares Switch-SWE with related benchmarks and gives harness, scoring, and context-manager implementation details with worked trajectory examples.

repos.title: Sheaf-MPNN: A Library for Sheaf Neural Networks as Message Passing
repos.paper_summary: Sheaf-MPNN is a PyTorch Geometric library that implements sheaf neural networks (SNNs) as local message passing, avoiding construction of the global sheaf Laplacian. It covers fifteen SNN families with homogeneous and heterogeneous variants, directed and undirected settings, and diagonal, general, orthogonal, and low-rank restriction maps. Each layer transports node states into edge stalks through restriction maps, computes an interaction function, pulls messages back, and aggregates them at nodes. The authors prove (Theorem 1 and appendix results) that architectures including Neural Sheaf Diffusion, standard MPNNs, SheafAN, and Neural Sheaf Propagation admit this message-passing form with matching normalization. The paper also provides a benchmarking suite covering more than 20 datasets for node- and graph-level tasks, heterogeneous graphs, and efficiency. The stated cost of the local computation is O(|E| d² f) operations and O(|E| d² + |E| d f + n d f) memory when messages are materialised, excluding map prediction and normalization. The paper does not report measured speedups or accuracy numbers in the text provided, so the efficiency benefit remains unverified here. Limitations stated by the authors: practical efficiency depends on the implementation and must be evaluated empirically, and the equivalence results are theoretical.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Sheaf networks assemble a global sparse operator, and the authors propose local message passing instead.

digest_headlines.heading: Sheaf Message Passing in a Nutshell
digest_headlines.headline: Sheaf message passing recovers sheaf diffusion and standard message-passing networks as special cases of one general update.

digest_headlines.heading: Library Design and Usage
digest_headlines.headline: Sheaf-MPNN exposes sheaf layers and end-to-end models through one PyTorch Geometric interface with a command-line tool.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Software
digest_headlines.headline: Existing sheaf implementations usually cover single architectures and rely on explicitly assembled Laplacians.

digest_headlines.heading: Availability
digest_headlines.headline: The library is public under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license, with documentation and tutorial notebooks.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers sheaf background, the Sheaf Neural Network literature, model options, experiment tooling, and reproducibility.

repos.title: Turbo-GMM: FlashAttention-Inspired GPU-Accelerated Gaussian Mixture Model
repos.paper_summary:
Turbo-GMM is a fused GPU expectation-maximization kernel for diagonal-covariance Gaussian mixture models. When the full component axis fits on chip beside a tile of data points, it computes responsibility normalization and sufficient-statistic accumulation in one traversal of the components, so the input is read once and component scores are not recomputed. When it does not fit, a two-pass fallback is used. The paper proves in real arithmetic that both forms reproduce the standard EM updates for arbitrary tilings. Under its memory-traffic model, the single-sweep form moves Θ(Nd+Kd) elements when P·K is O(N+K), where P is the number of programs.

On an NVIDIA A100 across sixteen configurations, the median speedup over Flash-GMM is 2.15×, with up to 5.3× over PyTorch and 9.9× over scikit-learn. Peak memory drops by up to 338× relative to materializing implementations. The single-sweep path applies on this device only for K≤128 at d=32. The two-pass fallback is slower than Flash-GMM at K=512 and K=1024, and the paper does not identify the cause. All measurements come from one GPU, one seeded dataset and one shared initialization.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Turbo-GMM fuses EM so one sweep over components completes responsibility normalization and statistic accumulation, removing a second score recomputation.

digest_headlines.heading: Background and the Standard Implementation
digest_headlines.headline: The baseline EM iteration expresses scores as one bilinear product, and its dataflow determines whether it can be fused.

digest_headlines.heading: Method
digest_headlines.headline: Turbo-GMM completes normalization and statistic accumulation in one tile visit when the whole component axis fits on chip.

digest_headlines.heading: Exactness and Cost
digest_headlines.headline: Both fused forms match standard EM in real arithmetic for any tiling and are costed under an explicit traffic model.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On sixteen shapes, Turbo-GMM gives a median 2.15× speedup over Flash-GMM, with the advantage depending on on-chip residency.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior online-softmax and fused EM work supplies the merge rule and the two-sweep design; the single sweep is claimed to have no precedent.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion
digest_headlines.headline: The single sweep, not fusion alone, decides latency, and its benefit is bounded by on-chip capacity on one A100.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Turbo-GMM avoids the responsibility matrix and completes EM in one traversal when the component axis fits, with latency gains conditional on shape.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers usage disclosure, the two-pass construction, proofs, and the Flash-GMM benchmarking protocol.
